summary: Selling a medical billing company? See what buyers look for in 2027, from client mix to collections data, and how to prepare before year-end.
body_markdown:
A medical billing company for sale will be evaluated more than its revenue or reported profit. Buyers want to understand whether earnings are sustainable, clients are likely to stay, operations are documented, and the business can continue performing after the owner steps away.


Valuation methods differ across published sources, so owners should understand the factors and assumptions behind any estimated business value.


This blog explains what buyers look for in a medical billing company,


how they evaluate financial health and operational performance,


and what owners should organize before year-end. For additional guidance, see medical billing business M&A 2027.


## What Buyers Look for in a Medical Billing Company


at a Glance


Buyers typically evaluate six key areas. How you rate on each one shapes both interest and price.

- **Recurring revenue:** Stable monthly revenue from recurring client relationships.


- **Client distribution:** A spread of clients, specialties, and payers, with no single client carrying out the business.


- **Collections performance:** Strong revenue cycle management results that can be proven from your system.


- **Technology:** Optimized workflows, automation, and working integrations with client EHR and PM systems.


- **Compliance:** A documented HIPAA program signed by BAAs and evidence of security controls.


- **People:** A team that manages daily operations without constant owner oversight.


The following sections explain why each factor matters and what evidence buyers expect to review.


## Revenue Quality and Client Mix


Buyers value revenue that is likely to continue after the sale. Recurring revenue from signed contracts is worth more than the same dollars from month-to-month or handshake clients.


Expect questions on:


- **Contract terms:** Length, renewal dates, termination notice, and whether a sale needs client consent.


- **Client retention:** How many clients you kept, lost, and added each year, and why the lost ones left.


- **Specialty and payer mix:** Whether revenue depends on one specialty or payer, that could change.


Client concentration


gets extra attention. If one client makes up a large share of revenue, losing that client after the sale would hit the buyer hard. Many buyers set a limit on how much revenue any client can represent, and above it they may lower the price, shift part of it into an earn-out, or ask for added protections.


## Operational Performance Buyers Can Verify


Every seller says their collections are strong. Buyers want proof, so they will ask for reports and then rebuild the numbers from your billing system during due diligence.


The core metrics are:


- **Clean claim rate:** Share of claims accepted on first submission.


- **Denial rate:** Share of claims denied, and how quickly denials are worked.


- **Days in A/R:** How long does it take clients to get paid.


- **Net collection rate:** How much of the collectible amount is actually collected.


Report each metric by client rather than relying only on company-wide totals, as strong averages can hide underperforming accounts that buyers may identify during due diligence. Make sure reports are reproducible by pulling metrics directly from your system, using consistent definitions, and saving monthly snapshots.


## Technology, Compliance and People


### Technology


Buyers look at how much of your work is automated and how well you connect to client EHR and practice management systems. Manual, one-off workflows raise integration costs after the sale.


### Compliance


A billing company handles protected health information every day, so compliance is a core diligence item. Buyers will review your HIPAA program, risk assessments, policies, and staff training records.


They’ll also check that every client has a signed business associate agreement (BAA). A SOC 2 report or similar independent audit gives buyers outside evidence that your controls work.


### People


If you use offshore or blended staffing, buyers will review data security, oversight, and contractual arrangements. They want assurance that service quality remains consistent across all locations


Finally, consider key-person risk. If the owner personally handles major client relationships, approves billing decisions, or resolves daily operational problems, the business may be harder to transition. Documented responsibilities and capable managers help show that the company can operate without constant owner involvement.


## Medical Billing Company Valuation: How the Number Is Built


Most medical billing company valuation work starts with earnings. Buyers of larger companies usually work from


**adjusted EBITDA (E** arnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization), adjusted for costs a new owner won’t carry. Smaller deals may use owner’s earnings instead, this helps explain why valuation estimates for medical billing companies vary across sources.


Adjustments, or add-backs, might include one-time legal fees or owner pay above a market salary. Each one needs documentation, because buyers will test it.


Many buyers test your earnings with a


**quality of earnings (QoE)** review. Commissioning a sell-side QoE before going to market lets you find and fix issues first.


The buyer then applies a multiple to those earnings. Factors that tend to move the multiple:

Your actual number depends on your financials, the buyer, and the deal structure, which is best reviewed privately.


## How to Prepare a


Medical Billing Company for Sale


Owners considering a sale within the next 12 to 24 months can use year-end to organize financial records, address business weaknesses, and review overall performance.


Preparing early gives the company time to document improvements and resolve issues before a buyer begins reviewing the business.


Use this list:


- **Close the year’s financials cleanly:** Reconcile accounts, separate personal expenses, and move to accrual-basis books if your CPA recommends it.


- **Review contracts and BAAs:** Confirm that every client has a signed, current agreement and BAA, and note renewal dates and change-of-control terms.


- **Make a client concentration plan:** If one or two clients dominate revenue, grow other accounts and secure longer terms with the largest ones.


- **Build a KPI dashboard:** to track


clean claim rate, denial rate, days in A/R, and net collection rate by client, pulled directly from your system.


- **Document your SOPs:** Write down how billing, follow-up, reporting, and onboarding work.


- **Gather compliance evidence:** Collect your HIPAA risk assessment, policies, training logs, and any SOC 2 or similar reports.


- **Reduce owner dependency:** Hand client relationships and daily decisions to your team and show that the work holds up without you.


The goal is not to make every metric look perfect. It is to understand the company’s position, address preventable risks, and support important claims with reliable records.
